one_liner: SAX-style CommonMark parser in C, no AST, beats cmark on speed and memory when you don't need a DOM.
what_it_does: MD4C parses Markdown (CommonMark 0.31 compliant, with optional GFM-ish extensions like tables, strikethrough, footnotes, tasklists) and calls your callbacks on block/span enter/leave and text chunks — there is no tree to walk. `md_parse()` is the whole parser API; `md_html()` (separate md4c-html library) renders straight to HTML if that's all you need. It is not a drop-in for cmark's API: cmark builds and exposes an AST, MD4C only pushes events, so callers wanting a tree must build one themselves.
how_it_is_fast: No AST allocation: nodes/spans are never materialized as heap objects, they're reported directly as callback events with pointers into the original input buffer plus a length (strings aren't even zero-terminated, avoiding a copy). This is why realloc() calls on the Pro-Git benchmark are 36 for MD4C vs 1,304,578 for cmark, and heap peak is ~1.8x lower. The parser is also written for linear/near-linear time on adversarial input, with a pathological-input test suite (test/pathological-tests.py) guarding against the quadratic blowups some Markdown parsers hit.
when_to_use: You only need HTML (or another flat format) output and don't need to inspect/mutate a parsed document tree
You're parsing large or many documents and cmark's AST allocation overhead (memory, realloc churn) is the bottleneck
You want a single-header/single-source C library to vendor with zero dependencies beyond libc
Input may be adversarial or untrusted and you want protection against quadratic-time pathological Markdown
You're fine writing your own callback-based renderer instead of consuming a ready-made tree
when_not_to_use: You need a DOM/AST to transform, query, or re-serialize the document (MD4C has no tree; you'd build and maintain your own)
You need GFM tables/strikethrough/tasklists out of the box without opting into extension flags — CommonMark-only by default
Input isn't already validated UTF-8/ASCII-compatible and you care about malformed-input handling: MD4C does no input validation by design (GIGO) and will propagate ill-formed byte sequences verbatim

You're relying on the 2017 author benchmark as a rigorous head-to-head: CPU model and compiler flags are unstated, and it compares a SAX renderer against an AST-building parser, which the author himself calls an unfair memory comparison
You need runtime allocator customization or documented thread-safety guarantees — neither is documented in the public header

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C standard library
integration.min_toolchain: C (CMake >=3.14 for the provided build); no C standard version stated in README/CMakeLists beyond LANGUAGES C
integration.platforms: Windows and POSIX; README states other platforms should work if C stdlib with heap management is available
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same job (Markdown-to-HTML) but a different API shape than cmark; md_parse()/md_html() are callback-driven, not a parse-to-AST function, so callers of cmark's tree API must be rewritten

gotchas: Callback strings are not zero-terminated; you must use the supplied MD_SIZE length, not strlen()
No input validation: malformed UTF-8 is passed through to callbacks unchanged (GIGO philosophy), so validate upstream if that matters
Multiple heap-buffer-overflow CVEs were reported and fixed in 2018 (issues #36–#39); no similar reports found in more recent history via search
GFM-style tables, strikethrough, footnotes, tasklists, highlight/insert/spoiler spans etc. are all opt-in via MD_FLAG_* bits, not defaults
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet for Markdown specifically — the other markup-html-markdown entries (lexbor, html5-parser, MarkupEver, MyHTML, pugixml, roxmltree, selectolax, stb_xml) are HTML/XML parsers, not Markdown. Pick MD4C whenever the workload is Markdown-to-HTML (or Markdown-to-anything via callbacks) and you don't need a DOM.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run benchmark (2017) comparing MD4C's md2html CLI against the cmark CLI of that era, 10 runs each on tmpfs, on a 64-bit Slackware 14.2 Linux box with unstated CPU and compiler flags: MD4C ran 1.4x-7.7x faster depending on input shape and used ~1.8x less peak heap on a ~105MB Pro-Git Markdown compilation, with far fewer realloc() calls (36 vs 1,304,578) reflecting its no-AST design.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-17), MIT licensed, single C source/header pair small enough to vendor directly — low risk to adopt even without upstream support.
